name: Moon
description: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite and the fifth largest moon in the Solar System. It is the only extraterrestrial body on which humans have walked, with 12 Apollo astronauts landing between 1969 and 1972.
surface: Mare (seas of hardened lava), highlands, craters, mountains
formation: Giant impact hypothesis — a Mars-sized object struck Earth
first_human_landing: Apollo 11, July 20, 1969 — Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin
known_missions: Luna 2 — first spacecraft to impact the Moon (1959)
Artemis I (NASA, 2022) — uncrewed Orion test flight
highest_point: Selenean Summit — 10.78 km above mean radius
summary: The Moon is humanity's closest cosmic neighbor and first destination beyond Earth. Its regular gravitational pull creates Earth's tides and stabilizes our planet's axial tilt. The 12 Apollo astronauts who walked on the Moon between 1969–1972 brought back 382 kg of lunar rock, revolutionizing our understanding of the Solar System's history.
interesting_facts: The Moon is tidally locked — the same side always faces Earth
Moonquakes occur — the Moon is seismically active
The Moon is drifting away from Earth at 3.8 cm per year
The Moon has no global magnetic field, but some regions have remnant magnetism
Chandrayaan-3 (India) successfully landed at the lunar south pole in 2023 — first ever
The Moon's gravity causes Earth's tides
The Moon has water ice in permanently shadowed polar craters
Buzz Aldrin brought a piece of the Wright Brothers' plane to the Moon
The Moon's far side (dark side) was first photographed by Luna 3 in 1959
NASA's Artemis program aims to return humans to the Moon by the mid-2020s

faq.q: How far is the Moon from Earth?
faq.a: The Moon is on average 384,400 km from Earth. At its closest (perigee) it's 356,500 km, and at its farthest (apogee) 406,700 km. Light takes about 1.3 seconds to travel from Earth to the Moon.

Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon during NASA's Apollo program (1969–1972): Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, Pete Conrad, Alan Bean, Alan Shepard, Edgar Mitchell, David Scott, James Irwin, John Young, Charles Duke, Gene Cernan, and Harrison Schmitt.
Yes! Water ice has been confirmed in permanently shadowed craters at the lunar poles. India's Chandrayaan-1 detected it in 2008, and Chandrayaan-3 landed near the south pole in 2023.

faq.q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
faq.a: The Moon is tidally locked to Earth — its rotation period exactly matches its orbital period (both ~27.3 days), so the same hemisphere always faces Earth. We can see about 59% of the Moon over time due to wobbling (libration).
The most accepted theory is the Giant Impact Hypothesis: about 4.5 billion years ago, a Mars-sized body called Theia collided with the early Earth, ejecting debris that coalesced into the Moon.

faq.q: What is gravity like on the Moon?
faq.a: The Moon's gravity is 1.62 m/s² — about 1/6 of Earth's gravity. A 70 kg person would weigh only about 11.7 kg on the Moon.
The Moon has a diameter of 3,475 km — about 27% of Earth's diameter. It's the fifth largest moon in the Solar System.

faq.q: What is on the surface of the Moon?
faq.a: The Moon's surface has highlands (heavily cratered ancient crust), mare (dark plains of solidified ancient lava), mountains, valleys (rilles), and billions of craters from meteorite impacts.

faq.q: Will humans return to the Moon?
faq.a: Yes! NASA's Artemis program aims to return astronauts to the Moon, targeting the south pole. Artemis III is planned to land the first woman and next man on the Moon.

faq.q: Does the Moon have an atmosphere?
faq.a: The Moon has an extremely thin exosphere — a few scattered gas molecules. It has no real atmosphere, which means no weather, no wind, and extreme temperature variations.
